tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 56-year-old woman who is a long-time patient returns to the office for scheduled follow up of her type 2 diabetes and chronically elevated blood glucose. At her last visit 3 months ago, her HbA1C was 7.6%, where it had been for several visits. You recommended beginning treatment with insulin, which she refused because of her fear of needles. You then increased her dose of glimepiride from 4 mg to 8 mg once a day and advised her to more strictly follow her diet and exercise regimen, which she claims to be doing. Since the last visit, her home fingerstick glucose levels have ranged from 119 mg/dL to 263 mg/dL (6.6 to 14.6 mmol/L) and her weight on her home scale is unchanged at about 98 kg. She describes increased thirst and urination but denies blurry vision, nonhealing ulcers, or lethargy.

Per office protocol, a fingerstick glucose test on arrival today shows glucose level of 221mg/dL (12.27 mmol/L) and hemoglobin A1C 8.1%; urine dipstick is normal.

Review of Systems:
General: Increased thirst and is drinking more water. Appetite is normal and her weight at home has been unchanged for several months. She denies lethargy, fever, chills, or night sweats.

Skin: No rash, pruritus, or lesions

HEENT: No change in vision, sore throat, dysphagia

Pulmonary: No cough, shortness of breath, wheezing

Cardiovascular: No chest pain, pressure, or discomfort; no orthopnea, dyspnea on exertion, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

Gastrointestinal: No abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea

Genitourinary: Increased urinary frequency without urgency, dysuria, or blood in urine. No vaginal discharge or itching.

Musculoskeletal: No joint or muscle pain, no sores or lesions on feet.

Neurologic: Has numbness and tingling in both feet that comes and goes throughout the day. No headache, tremor, change in gait.

Psychiatric: No mood swings, depression, or anxiety.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and obesity

Surgical history: Cholecystectomy 5 years prior

Medications: Metformin 1000 mg twice a day, atorvastatin 80 mg once a day, glimepiride 8 mg once a day with breakfast, lisinopril 40 mg once a day, all of which she claims to be taking faithfully.

Allergies: Penicillin, which causes rash

Family history: Father died from myocardial infarction at age 89 years, mother age 88 years has type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.

Social history: Patient works as a social worker, has never smoked cigarettes, denies any illicit drug use, drinks 1 to 2 glasses of wine with dinner every night. She rides a stationary bike about 1 to 2 days per week for 20 minutes, which she has been able to do without difficulty. She is up to date with all immunizations. Her diet consists mainly of pizza, chicken, vegetables, fruit, pasta, and diet sodas. She is married and has a 12-year-old son. She is intermittently sexually active with her husband 1 to 2 times per month. They do not use contraception as she is no longer menstruating.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Well-appearing female in no apparent distress, height 1.65 m, weight 95.3 kg (BMI 34.9)

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 82 min
BP: 159/88 mmHg
Respirations: 12/min

Skin: There is velvety smooth hyperpigmentation in neck folds and under arms; no other lesions or rash.

HEENT: Moist mucous membranes, no exudates, no cervical lymphadenopathy.

Pulmonary: Clear to auscultation bilaterally, no wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Jugular venous distention normal.

Gastrointestinal: Obese abdomen, soft, non-distended, normal bowel sounds, no rebound or guarding.

Genitourinary: No signs of yeast infection or other lesions. No tenderness to flank percussion.

Musculoskeletal: No peripheral edema, swelling or tenderness. Joints full range of motion and nontender.

Neurologic: Decreased sensation to light touch in feet bilaterally. Cranial nerves II to VIII grossly intact, normal gait, strength 5/5 throughout.

Mental status: Alert and oriented x3

Test Results:
Results of appropriate testing return and are shown:

Serum

HbA1C: 8.1%
Glucose: 221 mg/dL (12.27 mmol/L)
Sodium: 138 mEq/L (138 mmol/L)
Potassium: 4.1 mEq/L (4.1 mmol/L)
Creatinine: 0.7 mg/dL ( 62 µmol/L)
BUN: 23 mg/dL (8.2 mmol/L)
Lipid Panel: Results pending
sc_draft_1:
Age: 56  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Follow-up for type 2 diabetes with elevated HbA1C (8.1%) and glucose (221 mg/dL), increased thirst and urination, and peripheral neuropathy symptoms.  
Analysis: The patient has long-standing type 2 diabetes with suboptimal glycemic control despite metformin and high-dose glimepiride (8 mg daily). HbA1C has risen from 7.6% to 8.1% over 3 months, with home glucose readings ranging from 119 to 263 mg/dL. She reports polydipsia and polyuria, consistent with hyperglycemia, but no signs of diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (normal mental status, no vomiting, normal electrolytes). Physical exam reveals acanthosis nigricans and decreased sensation in both feet, indicating diabetic neuropathy. Blood pressure is elevated at 159/88 mmHg despite lisinopril 40 mg daily. Differential considerations include progressive beta-cell failure, suboptimal adherence (though she claims adherence), dietary/lifestyle factors (including regular alcohol intake), and possible secondary causes of hyperglycemia. The main challenge is intensifying therapy given her needle phobia and refusal of insulin at the prior visit.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Lipid panel (pending), urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, and referral for dilated fundoscopic examination.  
Conclusion: This is a non-emergent visit for poorly controlled type 2 diabetes complicated by neuropathy and hypertension. The primary issues are intensification of glycemic control and optimization of blood pressure.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  
Recommendations:  
1. Re-discuss insulin therapy, addressing needle phobia (e.g., insulin pens, ultra-fine needles, education). Given HbA1C >8%, initiate basal insulin (e.g., long-acting analog) at a low dose (e.g., 10 units daily) and titrate based on fasting glucose. If insulin is refused, consider adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor; reduce glimepiride dose to 4 mg if adding an agent with hypoglycemia risk.  
2. Optimize blood pressure: lisinopril is at maximum dose; add amlodipine or a thiazide diuretic. Target BP <130/80 mmHg.  
3. Reinforce lifestyle modifications: reduce refined carbohydrates and alcohol intake (limit to <1 drink/day), increase physical activity (currently only 1–2 days/week).  
4. Manage neuropathic symptoms: consider gabapentin or pregabalin if bothersome; emphasize daily foot inspection and proper foot care.  
5. Obtain lipid panel results and continue atorvastatin 80 mg; adjust if needed.  
6. Screen for diabetic complications: urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, dilated eye exam, and periodic foot exams.  
7. Provide diabetes self-management education and referral to a nutritionist.  
8. Monitor glucose logs and adjust therapy at follow-up in 2–3 months.  
Notes: None

Age: 28 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Sudden severe left-sided pelvic pain with lightheadedness, 7 weeks amenorrhea, positive pregnancy test, signs of shock.  
Analysis: The patient presents with acute pelvic pain, hemodynamic instability (tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, diaphoresis), and peritoneal signs. She has a history of prior ectopic pregnancy and pelvic inflammatory disease. Positive beta-hCG (4,200 mIU/mL) with an empty uterus, complex left adnexal mass with ring-of-fire sign, and significant free fluid in pelvis and Morison's pouch indicate a ruptured ectopic pregnancy with intra-abdominal hemorrhage. Hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL confirms significant blood loss. Differential includes ruptured ovarian cyst, tubo-ovarian abscess, or appendicitis, but the combination of pregnancy, adnexal mass, free fluid, and shock strongly favors ruptured ectopic pregnancy.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None additional; bedside ultrasound and labs already performed. Crossmatch and coagulation studies may be obtained but are not delaying surgery.  
Conclusion: Ruptured left tubal ectopic pregnancy with hemorrhagic shock and acute blood loss anemia.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology  
Recommendations: Immediate emergent laparotomy (already alerted). Administer O-negative packed red blood cells and initiate massive transfusion protocol if needed. Continue fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids. Prepare for surgical control of bleeding (salpingectomy or salpingostomy). Monitor vital signs and urine output. Postoperatively, follow serial beta-hCG until negative. Provide Rho(D) immune globulin if Rh-negative (blood type not specified; O-negative ordered suggests possible Rh-negative status). Consider ICU admission for hemodynamic monitoring.  
Notes: The patient is in hypovolemic shock; do not delay surgery for further imaging. Ensure availability of blood products and surgical team.

Analysis: The patient presents with classic features of a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Strong supporting facts include: 7 weeks amenorrhea with positive beta-hCG (4,200 mIU/mL), empty uterus on ultrasound, complex left adnexal mass with ring-of-fire sign, significant free fluid in the pelvis and Morison's pouch (indicating hemoperitoneum), and hemodynamic instability (HR 132, BP 78/48) with pallor and diaphoresis. Hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL confirms significant blood loss. Her history of prior left tubal ectopic pregnancy and pelvic inflammatory disease are major risk factors. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
case_text:
Vignette:
A 42-year-old man presents with mild low back ache that developed after spending several hours gardening yesterday. He was bending and lifting bags of soil. The pain is localized to the lower back and does not radiate to the legs. He denies numbness, tingling, weakness, or changes in bowel or bladder function. He has no history of prior back surgery or chronic back problems. On examination, there is mild paraspinal muscle tenderness in the lumbar region bilaterally. Range of motion is mildly reduced on flexion. Straight leg raise is negative bilaterally. Neurological examination of the lower extremities is normal.
sc_draft_1:
Age: 42
Sex: Male
Complaint: Mild localized low back ache after gardening (bending and lifting), without radiation, neurologic symptoms, or bowel/bladder changes.
Analysis: The presentation is consistent with acute mechanical low back pain (lumbar strain) from physical exertion. Supporting facts include the clear precipitating activity (bending/lifting), localized pain without radicular features, negative straight leg raise bilaterally, normal lower-extremity neurologic examination, and absence of red flags (no numbness, tingling, weakness, or bowel/bladder dysfunction). The mild paraspinal tenderness and reduced flexion on range of motion are typical of musculoligamentous strain. Main differential considerations include lumbar disc herniation (unlikely given negative straight leg raise and normal neuro exam), lumbar spondylosis, and facet joint strain; however, no features suggest serious pathology such as fracture, infection, or cauda equina syndrome.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (imaging and laboratory studies are not indicated for acute non-specific low back pain without red flags).
Conclusion: Acute mechanical low back pain (lumbar strain) in a 42-year-old man with no red flags, radiculopathy, or neurologic deficit; a benign, self-limited condition.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Reassure the patient that this is a benign, self-limited condition. Advise continued gentle activity and avoidance of prolonged bed rest; recommend heat application to the lumbar region for comfort. Suggest over-the-counter analgesics such as acetaminophen or NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) if tolerated and no contraindications. Instruct the patient to return or seek care if he develops leg pain or weakness, numbness/tingling, or bowel/bladder dysfunction, or if pain worsens or fails to improve within a few weeks. Encourage gradual resumption of normal activities and proper lifting technique to prevent recurrence.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[2]
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old man who jogs regularly presents with a 1-week history of an itchy rash in his groin folds. He reports the itch worsens after running and sweating. He denies any genital lesions, urinary symptoms, or prior similar episodes. On examination, there are bilateral, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with slightly raised scaly borders along the inguinal creases extending to the proximal inner thighs. The scrotum is spared. There is no central clearing or satellite lesions. No inguinal lymphadenopathy is appreciated.

Age: 35  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Itchy rash in groin folds for 1 week, worsening after running and sweating.  
Analysis: The presentation of bilateral, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with raised scaly borders along the inguinal creases, sparing the scrotum, and itch exacerbated by sweating is highly characteristic of tinea cruris (jock itch). The absence of central clearing or satellite lesions does not exclude this diagnosis, as these features are not always present. Differential considerations include inverse psoriasis (typically more symmetric, less scaly, and often involves the scrotum), candidal intertrigo (often with satellite pustules and more moist appearance), erythrasma (coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp), and contact dermatitis (history of irritant exposure). No lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms suggests a localized, non-invasive process.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Skin scraping for potassium hydroxide (KOH) wet mount microscopy; fungal culture if KOH is negative or diagnosis uncertain.  
Conclusion: Likely tinea cruris (dermatophytosis) based on clinical morphology and location.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  
Recommendations: Initiate topical antifungal therapy (e.g., clotrimazole, terbinafine, or miconazole) applied to the affected area and a margin of surrounding skin for 2–4 weeks, continuing for at least 1 week after symptom resolution. Advise keeping the groin area clean and dry, wearing loose-fitting cotton underwear, changing clothes promptly after exercise, and using antifungal powder as adjunctive measure. If no improvement after 2 weeks of treatment, reassess for alternative diagnoses (e.g., inverse psoriasis, erythrasma) and consider fungal culture. Avoid topical corticosteroids unless a non-fungal cause is confirmed, as they can worsen tinea.  
Notes: Scrotal sparing is typical for tinea cruris; absence of central clearing does not rule out the diagnosis. If lesions fail to respond to appropriate antifungal therapy, consider referral to dermatology for further evaluation.

tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old female soccer player presents to the sports medicine clinic two days after sustaining a left knee injury during a game. She reports that while pivoting to change direction she felt a sudden pop in her knee followed by immediate swelling and inability to continue playing. She was unable to bear full weight and has been using crutches since. She denies any prior knee injuries. On examination, there is a moderate effusion of the left knee. Range of motion is limited by pain and swelling. The Lachman test is positive with a soft endpoint on the left, and the anterior drawer test demonstrates increased anterior tibial translation compared to the right. McMurray test is equivocal. The collateral ligaments are stable. She is neurovascularly intact distally.
sc_draft_1:
Age: 22
Sex: Female
Complaint: Left knee injury with sudden pop, immediate swelling, inability to bear weight, and instability after a pivoting movement.
Analysis: The mechanism (pivoting with a pop), acute effusion, positive Lachman test with a soft endpoint, and increased anterior drawer translation strongly indicate an acute anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear. The equivocal McMurray test raises the possibility of a concurrent meniscal injury, though collateral ligaments are stable and distal neurovascular status is intact. Differential considerations include meniscal tear, patellar dislocation, or collateral ligament injury, but the Lachman and drawer findings are most specific for ACL rupture.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI of the left knee to confirm ACL tear and evaluate for meniscal or chondral injury; plain radiographs (X-ray) to rule out associated fractures or avulsions.
Conclusion: Acute left ACL rupture is highly likely, with possible meniscal involvement; neurovascular status is intact.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Initiate RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation) and continue protected weight-bearing with crutches. Provide a knee immobilizer or brace for comfort. Refer the patient to an orthopedic surgeon for further evaluation. Obtain MRI to confirm the diagnosis and assess for meniscal injury. Discuss treatment options (surgical reconstruction vs. conservative rehabilitation) based on patient activity level and goals. Begin early physical therapy for range of motion and quadriceps strengthening once swelling subsides.
Notes: None

Analysis: The mechanism of injury (pivoting with a sudden pop), immediate effusion (suggesting hemarthrosis), and inability to continue playing are highly consistent with an acute anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear. The equivocal McMurray test raises the possibility of a concurrent meniscal injury, though it is not definitive. Stable collateral ligaments and intact distal neurovascular status help narrow the differential. Main differential considerations include ACL tear (most likely), meniscal tear, patellar dislocation, and tibial plateau fracture; the latter is less likely given the mechanism and stable exam but should be excluded.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Plain radiographs (AP, lateral, and tunnel views) to rule out associated fractures or Segond fracture; MRI of the left knee to confirm the ACL tear and evaluate for meniscal, chondral, or collateral ligament injuries.
Conclusion: Acute left knee injury with clinical findings strongly suggestive of a complete anterior cruciate ligament tear, with possible associated meniscal injury. The knee is otherwise stable in the collateral ligaments and neurovascularly intact.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Continue protected weight-bearing with crutches and use a knee immobilizer or hinged brace for comfort. Apply ice, elevation, and compression to manage swelling. Arrange for plain radiographs to exclude fracture, followed by MRI to confirm the ACL tear and assess for meniscal damage. Refer to an orthopedic surgeon for definitive management planning, including discussion of surgical reconstruction versus conservative rehabilitation based on the patient's activity level and goals. Provide analgesia as needed and schedule close follow-up.
Notes: The equivocal McMurray test warrants careful MRI evaluation for a meniscal tear, as this may influence surgical decision-making. Immediate hemarthrosis within hours of injury strongly supports an intra-articular ligamentous injury rather than a simple sprain.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
case_text:
Vignette:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his mother who noticed patches of hair loss on his scalp over the past 3 weeks. The patches have been gradually enlarging and the affected areas appear scaly. He attends elementary school and his mother reports several classmates have had similar issues. He denies pain but admits to mild itching. On examination, there are two well-defined round patches of alopecia on the parietal and occipital scalp, measuring approximately 3 cm and 2 cm in diameter respectively. Within the patches, the hair shafts are broken off at the surface giving a black-dot appearance. The surrounding scalp is covered with fine gray-white scale. There is mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. A Wood lamp examination reveals no fluorescence. KOH preparation of plucked hairs shows endothrix spores surrounding and within the hair shaft.
sc_draft_1:
Age: 6 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Gradually enlarging, scaly patches of hair loss on the scalp for 3 weeks, with mild itching and broken-off hair shafts.
Analysis: The clinical presentation of well-defined round patches of alopecia with broken hairs at the surface (black-dot appearance), fine gray-white scaling, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy is highly consistent with tinea capitis. The KOH preparation showing endothrix spores within and around the hair shaft confirms a fungal etiology (endothrix infection, most commonly Trichophyton tonsurans). The absence of fluorescence on Wood lamp examination is typical for endothrix (non-fluorescent) infections, distinguishing it from ectothrix Microsporum species that fluoresce. The history of affected classmates supports contagious spread. Differential considerations include alopecia areata (typically non-scaly, no broken hairs, no adenopathy), trichotillomania (irregular patches, no scale), and seborrheic dermatitis (diffuse scaling without black dots). The strongest supporting facts are the black-dot appearance, scaly patches, lymphadenopathy, and positive KOH for endothrix spores.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Fungal culture of plucked hairs or scale to identify the causative species and guide therapy (optional but useful); no other equipment needed as diagnosis is confirmed by KOH.
Conclusion: Tinea capitis (endothrix type, likely Trichophyton tonsurans) in a 6-year-old boy, presenting with black-dot alopecia, scaling, and regional lymphadenopathy.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Initiate systemic oral antifungal therapy (e.g., griseofulvin or terbinafine) for 4–8 weeks, as topical agents alone are ineffective for endothrix infection. Adjunctive use of a ketoconazole or selenium sulfide shampoo 2–3 times weekly can reduce shedding of infectious spores. Evaluate and treat household contacts and close classmates who are symptomatic. Advise against sharing combs, brushes, hats, and pillows; wash linens and personal items. Schedule follow-up to monitor response and ensure completion of therapy. Address the mother's concerns regarding contagiousness and school attendance.
Notes: Topical therapy alone is insufficient for endothrix tinea capitis; systemic treatment is mandatory. Wood lamp non-fluorescence does not exclude tinea capitis, as Trichophyton tonsurans does not fluoresce.

Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics

Discharge with clear instructions to return immediately if swelling worsens, breathing becomes difficult, or any other systemic symptoms appear. Consider referral to an allergist for venom allergy testing and discussion of an epinephrine auto-injector, given the potential for more severe reactions with future stings.
Notes: Bee sting reactions can occasionally progress to anaphylaxis; caregivers should be educated on warning signs and the use of an epinephrine auto-injector if prescribed. None otherwise.

Analysis: The clinical picture is classic for a thrombosed external hemorrhoid. The acute onset after straining, constant throbbing pain, and the presence of a tense, bluish-purple, spherical, tender nodule at the anal verge are highly specific. The absence of fever, purulent drainage, and erythema argues against an infectious process such as a perianal abscess. The patient's risk factors (prolonged sitting, low-fiber diet, poor fluid intake, prior hemorrhoidal symptoms) support this diagnosis. Differential considerations include perianal abscess (excluded by lack of systemic signs and erythema), anal fissure (typically associated with sharp pain during defecation, not a constant lump), and prolapsed internal hemorrhoid (usually reducible and less acutely painful). Digital rectal exam is deferred due to pain, but is not essential for diagnosis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (clinical diagnosis is sufficient; no imaging or laboratory tests are indicated).

- Advise the patient to avoid prolonged sitting; recommend frequent breaks and use of a donut cushion while driving.
- If pain is severe or persists beyond 48-72 hours, or if the patient prefers immediate relief, consider surgical excision (thrombectomy) under local anesthesia, which provides faster symptom resolution than conservative care.
- Educate on lifestyle modifications: high-fiber diet, adequate hydration, regular exercise, and avoiding straining during bowel movements to prevent recurrence.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
case_text:
Vignette:
A 22-year-old student presents with a 5-year history of worsening nasal congestion, sneezing, and nasal itching. Symptoms are year-round but worse during the spring season. On further questioning it is revealed that he has significant eye itching, redness, and tearing as well as palate and throat itching during the spring season. He remembers that his mother told him at some point that he used to have eczema in infancy.

Age: 22  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: 5-year history of worsening nasal congestion, sneezing, and nasal itching, year-round but worse in spring, accompanied by eye itching, redness, tearing, and palate/throat itching during spring.  
Analysis: The patient's chronic nasal symptoms with seasonal exacerbation, ocular and oropharyngeal itching, and history of infantile eczema strongly suggest allergic rhinitis (seasonal and perennial) with associated allergic conjunctivitis. The atopic background (eczema) supports an IgE-mediated mechanism. Differential considerations include non-allergic rhinitis, chronic sinusitis, and nasal polyps, but the combination of symptoms and atopy makes allergic rhinitis the most likely diagnosis.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Allergy testing (skin prick test or serum specific IgE) to identify triggers; nasal endoscopy to exclude structural abnormalities if indicated.  
Conclusion: Allergic rhinitis (seasonal and perennial) with associated allergic conjunctivitis.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)  
Recommendations: Recommend allergen avoidance (e.g., pollen, dust mites), intranasal corticosteroids, oral antihistamines, and antihistamine eye drops for ocular symptoms. Consider referral to allergy/immunology for allergen immunotherapy if symptoms are not controlled. Address spring exacerbation with pre-seasonal medication.  
Notes: None  
Protocol Author: deepseekv4_default

Complaint: 5-year history of worsening nasal congestion, sneezing, nasal itching, with seasonal exacerbation in spring accompanied by eye itching, redness, tearing, and palate/throat itching.  
Analysis: The patient’s symptoms are consistent with allergic rhinitis, supported by the perennial nature with spring exacerbation, associated ocular and oropharyngeal itching, and a history of infantile eczema (atopic diathesis). The combination of nasal, ocular, and palatal symptoms strongly suggests an IgE-mediated allergic response. Differential considerations include non-allergic rhinitis (e.g., vasomotor rhinitis), chronic sinusitis, and nasal polyps, but the atopic history and symptom pattern favor allergic rhinitis with allergic conjunctivitis.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Allergy testing (skin prick test or serum specific IgE), nasal endoscopy (if structural abnormalities or polyps suspected), and possibly conjunctival examination.  
Conclusion: Allergic rhinitis (perennial with seasonal exacerbation) with associated allergic conjunctivitis, in a patient with an atopic background.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)  
Recommendations: Refer to an allergist or ENT specialist for confirmatory allergy testing. Initiate intranasal corticosteroids and oral or intranasal antihistamines for symptom control. Consider allergen avoidance measures (e.g., dust mite control, pollen avoidance during spring). For ocular symptoms, recommend preservative-free artificial tears and topical antihistamine/mast cell stabilizer eye drops. Evaluate for asthma, as atopic patients are at increased risk.  
Notes: None

Analysis: The clinical picture is highly consistent with allergic rhinitis (rhinoconjunctivitis). Year-round symptoms suggest sensitization to perennial allergens (e.g., dust mites), while spring worsening with eye, palate, and throat itching points to seasonal pollen allergy. The history of infantile eczema indicates an atopic predisposition (atopic march). Differential considerations include non-allergic (vasomotor) rhinitis, chronic rhinosinusitis, and nasal polyposis; however, the combination of nasal, ocular, and oropharyngeal itching with an atopic background strongly favors allergic etiology.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Skin prick testing to aeroallergens (perennial and seasonal) or specific IgE (ImmunoCAP) panel; anterior rhinoscopy/nasal endoscopy to assess nasal mucosa and exclude polyps.
Conclusion: Allergic rhinoconjunctivitis with perennial symptoms and prominent seasonal (spring/pollen) exacerbation in an atopic young adult.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Initiate intranasal corticosteroids (e.g., fluticasone or mometasone) as first-line daily therapy; add second-generation oral antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine, loratadine) for symptom control; use antihistamine eye drops (e.g., olopatadine) for ocular symptoms; advise allergen avoidance measures (e.g., pollen avoidance in spring, dust mite precautions year-round); refer to an allergist for confirmatory skin prick testing and consideration of allergen immunotherapy (subcutaneous or sublingual) given the 5-year progressive course and seasonal impact.
Notes: None

Complaint: 5-year history of worsening nasal congestion, sneezing, and nasal itching, year-round but worse in spring, accompanied by eye itching, redness, tearing, and palate/throat itching during spring.
Analysis: The combination of chronic nasal symptoms (congestion, sneezing, itching) with ocular itching/redness/tearing and oropharyngeal itching, worsening in spring, in a patient with a history of infantile eczema, strongly suggests allergic rhinitis (seasonal with a perennial component) and allergic conjunctivitis. The atopic background (eczema in infancy) supports an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity. Differential considerations include non-allergic rhinitis (vasomotor, irritant), chronic sinusitis, nasal polyps, and mechanical obstruction; however, the specific symptom pattern and seasonal exacerbation point toward allergic etiology.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Skin prick testing or specific serum IgE (RAST) to common aeroallergens (spring pollens, dust mites, animal dander); anterior rhinoscopy or nasal endoscopy to exclude structural abnormalities; optionally, conjunctival examination for allergic conjunctivitis.
Conclusion: Allergic rhinitis (seasonal with perennial component) and allergic conjunctivitis in an atopic individual, likely triggered by spring pollens and possibly perennial allergens.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Initiate allergen avoidance measures (e.g., keep windows closed during high pollen season, use HEPA filters, wash bedding in hot water, avoid known triggers). Prescribe intranasal corticosteroids (e.g., fluticasone or mometasone) as first-line therapy, and add oral second-generation antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine, loratadine) for symptom control. For ocular symptoms, recommend topical antihistamine/mast-cell stabilizer eye drops (e.g., olopatadine). Consider leukotriene receptor antagonists (e.g., montelukast) if symptoms are poorly controlled or if asthma is suspected. Refer to an allergist for skin prick testing and consideration of allergen immunotherapy (subcutaneous or sublingual) for long-term management. Additionally, screen for asthma (history of wheezing, cough, or dyspnea) given the atopic background, and counsel on the natural history of allergic rhinitis.

Complaint: 5-year history of worsening nasal congestion, sneezing, and nasal itching, with spring-season exacerbation accompanied by eye itching, redness, tearing, and palate/throat itching.
Analysis: The clinical picture is highly consistent with allergic rhinitis (perennial with seasonal exacerbation in spring). Strong supporting facts include the classic nasal triad (congestion, sneezing, itching), associated ocular symptoms (allergic conjunctivitis) and oropharyngeal itching during the spring pollen season, and a personal history of infantile eczema indicating an atopic predisposition. Year-round symptoms suggest sensitization to perennial allergens (e.g., dust mites), with spring worsening pointing to pollen triggers. Main differential considerations include non-allergic (vasomotor) rhinitis, chronic rhinosinusitis, nasal polyposis, and rhinitis medicamentosa, though the atopic history and seasonal ocular/oral symptoms strongly favor allergic rhinitis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Anterior rhinoscopy or nasal endoscopy; skin prick testing or serum specific IgE (to pollens and perennial allergens such as dust mites); total IgE and peripheral eosinophil count.
Conclusion: Allergic rhinitis with seasonal (spring) exacerbation and associated allergic conjunctivitis in a young atopic male with a history of infantile eczema.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Refer to an ENT or allergy specialist for confirmatory testing and management. Advise allergen avoidance (e.g., pollen exposure reduction in spring, dust mite precautions). Initiate intranasal corticosteroids as first-line therapy for nasal symptoms; add oral second-generation antihistamines for symptom control. For ocular symptoms, recommend antihistamine/mast-cell stabilizer eye drops. Consider allergen immunotherapy (subcutaneous or sublingual) if symptoms are inadequately controlled or for long-term modification. Address the additional considerations: the history of infantile eczema warrants monitoring for atopic comorbidities (asthma, food allergy); educate the patient on proper nasal spray technique and medication adherence.
Notes: None

Criterion_uni:
[1]
tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[2]
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

[3]
tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[4]
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.
