tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
case_text:
Vignette:
A 45-year-old man presents with acute onset of pain and redness of the skin of his lower extremity. Low-grade fever is present and the pretibial area is erythematous, edematous, and tender.
sc_draft_1:
Age: 45
Sex: Male
Complaint: Acute onset of pain and redness of the skin of the lower extremity with low-grade fever; pretibial area is erythematous, edematous, and tender.
Analysis: The clinical picture of acute pain, erythema, edema, and tenderness localized to the pretibial area accompanied by low-grade fever is most consistent with acute bacterial cellulitis of the lower extremity. The strongest supporting facts are the acute onset, localized erythema and edema, tenderness, and associated fever. Main differential considerations include erysipelas (more superficial, sharply demarcated border), necrotizing fasciitis (severe pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity, bullae, crepitus), deep vein thrombosis (swelling without typical erythema/fever), and contact dermatitis (pruritus, no fever). The absence of systemic toxicity and the localized nature favor uncomplicated cellulitis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Complete blood count with differential; blood cultures if systemic signs are present; clinical assessment for demarcation, bullae, or crepitus; consider lower extremity ultrasound to rule out abscess or deep vein thrombosis if suspicion arises.
Conclusion: Acute bacterial cellulitis of the lower extremity (pretibial region) with low-grade fever, without evidence of necrotizing infection or systemic toxicity at presentation.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease
Recommendations: Initiate empiric oral antibiotic therapy covering Streptococcus and methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus (e.g., cephalexin or dicloxacillin); elevate the affected extremity to reduce edema; mark the border of erythema to monitor progression; advise return or urgent reassessment if fever worsens, pain becomes disproportionate, erythema spreads rapidly, or bullae/crepitus develop; follow up in 24–48 hours to assess response; consider IV antibiotics and admission if no improvement or if signs of systemic infection or necrotizing fasciitis emerge. Address additional considerations: evaluate for predisposing factors such as diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, or skin breaks (e.g., tinea pedis) and treat accordingly.
Notes: None

Vignette: A 63-year-old man sustained a cut on his hand while gardening. His immunization history is significant for not having received a complete tetanus immunization schedule. He presents with signs of generalized tetanus with trismus ("lock jaw"), which results in a grimace described as "risus sardonicus" (sardonic smile). Intermittent tonic contraction of his skeletal muscles causes intensely painful spasms, which last for minutes, during which he retains consciousness. The spasms are triggered by external (noise, light, drafts, physical contact) or internal stimuli, and as a result he is at the risk of sustaining fractures or developing rhabdomyolysis. The tetanic spasms also produce opisthotonus, board-like abdominal wall rigidity, dysphagia, and apneic periods due to contraction of the thoracic muscles and/or glottal or pharyngeal muscles. During a generalized spasm the patient arches his back, extends his legs, flexes his arms in abduction, and clenches his fists. Apnea results during some of the spasms. Autonomic overactivity initially manifests as irritability, restlessness, sweating, and tachycardia. Several days later this may present as hyperpyrexia, cardiac arrhythmias, labile hypertension, or hypotension.

- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
case_text:
Vignette:
A 63-year-old man sustained a cut on his hand while gardening. His immunization history is significant for not having received a complete tetanus immunization schedule. He presents with signs of generalized tetanus with trismus ("lock jaw"), which results in a grimace described as "risus sardonicus" (sardonic smile). Intermittent tonic contraction of his skeletal muscles causes intensely painful spasms, which last for minutes, during which he retains consciousness. The spasms are triggered by external (noise, light, drafts, physical contact) or internal stimuli, and as a result he is at the risk of sustaining fractures or developing rhabdomyolysis. The tetanic spasms also produce opisthotonus, board-like abdominal wall rigidity, dysphagia, and apneic periods due to contraction of the thoracic muscles and/or glottal or pharyngeal muscles. During a generalized spasm the patient arches his back, extends his legs, flexes his arms in abduction, and clenches his fists. Apnea results during some of the spasms. Autonomic overactivity initially manifests as irritability, restlessness, sweating, and tachycardia. Several days later this may present as hyperpyrexia, cardiac arrhythmias, labile hypertension, or hypotension.

Age: 63
Sex: Male
Complaint: Cut on hand while gardening with incomplete tetanus immunization, presenting with trismus ("lock jaw"), risus sardonicus, painful tonic muscle spasms triggered by stimuli, opisthotonus, dysphagia, apneic episodes, and autonomic overactivity (irritability, restlessness, sweating, tachycardia).
Analysis: The clinical picture is consistent with generalized tetanus. Strongest supporting facts: incomplete tetanus immunization history, a gardening hand wound (likely contaminated), trismus, risus sardonicus, intermittent painful tonic spasms with retained consciousness triggered by external/internal stimuli, opisthotonus, board-like abdominal rigidity, dysphagia, apneic periods from thoracic/glottal/pharyngeal muscle contraction, and autonomic overactivity. Differential considerations include strychnine poisoning, acute dystonic reactions, hypocalcemic tetany, and meningitis; however, the wound history, immunization gap, and characteristic spasm pattern strongly favor tetanus. The risk of fractures, rhabdomyolysis, apnea, and later autonomic instability (hyperpyrexia, arrhythmias, labile blood pressure) makes this life-threatening.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Clinical diagnosis is primary; no confirmatory test is required. Next steps: continuous cardiorespiratory and pulse oximetry monitoring, ECG for arrhythmias, serum creatine kinase (CK) to assess rhabdomyolysis, electrolytes (including calcium and magnesium), renal function tests, and wound culture (though often negative). Equipment: ICU monitoring, airway management and mechanical ventilation capability.
Conclusion: Generalized tetanus with severe tonic spasms, apnea, and autonomic instability in the setting of an inadequately immunized patient with a contaminated wound — a life-threatening emergency requiring urgent intensive care.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Admit immediately to the intensive care unit. Administer tetanus immune globulin (TIG) as soon as possible. Perform wound debridement. Start antibiotic therapy (metronidazole or penicillin). Control spasms with benzodiazepines and consider magnesium sulfate; use neuromuscular blockade and mechanical ventilation if apnea or respiratory compromise occurs. Minimize external stimuli (quiet, dark environment, gentle handling). Manage autonomic instability with appropriate agents (e.g., beta-blockers or labetalol for hypertension, atropine for bradycardia). Monitor for rhabdomyolysis (CK, renal function) and fractures. Complete the tetanus vaccination series after recovery. Provide supportive care including hydration and nutrition (consider enteral feeding given dysphagia).
Notes: Tetanus is a clinical diagnosis; wound cultures are often negative and should not delay treatment. The patient remains conscious during spasms, which are intensely painful. Autonomic dysfunction may develop days later and is a major cause of mortality. Airway protection and ventilatory support are critical given apneic episodes.

Supporting facts include the short duration, clear sputum, afebrile status, normal pulse, nontender cervical lymphadenopathy, slightly inflamed pharynx, clear chest, and absence of neck stiffness. Main differential considerations include viral rhinitis/pharyngitis, influenza, and other self-limiting viral syndromes; bacterial pharyngitis and lower respiratory tract infection are less likely given the findings.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (clinical diagnosis; no laboratory or imaging studies indicated at this time).
Conclusion: Acute uncomplicated viral upper respiratory tract infection in a stable, afebrile young adult. Self-limiting illness; antibiotics are not indicated.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Reassure the patient that this is a viral infection and antibiotics will not help and may cause side effects or resistance. Advise smoking cessation or reduction, as smoking prolongs and worsens respiratory symptoms. Notes: Address the patient's expectation regarding antibiotics explicitly, explaining why they are not appropriate here; emphasize antibiotic stewardship. Smoking (10 cigarettes/day) is a modifiable risk factor that should be addressed. None other.

A 19-year-old man presents with diffuse redness and small bumps on his neck that appeared shortly after shaving this morning. He reports a mild burning sensation. He used a new razor and shaved without moisturizing first. He denies any prior skin conditions or allergies. On examination, there is diffuse erythema with multiple small non-follicular papules along the anterior and lateral neck. There is no pustulation, vesiculation, or excoriation. Age: 19 years old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Diffuse redness and small bumps on the neck with mild burning sensation shortly after shaving with a new razor without moisturizing.
Analysis: The clinical presentation is consistent with irritant contact dermatitis (razor burn) triggered by mechanical friction and lack of skin preparation during shaving. The acute onset after shaving, absence of pustules, vesicles, or follicular orientation of papules, and lack of systemic signs support a superficial irritant reaction rather than an infectious or allergic process. Differential considerations include pseudofolliculitis barbae (typically follicular and often with ingrown hairs), contact allergic dermatitis (would require prior sensitization and often delayed onset), and bacterial folliculitis (would show pustules and follicular involvement). The absence of lymphadenopathy and deeper tissue involvement rules out cellulitis or abscess.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Irritant contact dermatitis (razor burn) of the neck, mild, without secondary infection or complications.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Advise the patient to avoid further shaving of the affected area until erythema and burning resolve. Use a clean, sharp razor and apply a moisturizing shaving cream or gel before shaving in the future. Gently cleanse the area with a mild, fragrance-free cleanser and apply a soothing, non-comedogenic moisturizer. Cool compresses may alleviate burning. Over-the-counter hydrocortisone 1% cream can be used briefly (up to 3–5 days) if itching or inflammation is bothersome. Avoid picking or scratching the papules. If symptoms worsen, develop pustules, or spread, seek medical evaluation.
Notes: None

Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.

The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 28-yr-old man comes to the outpatient clinic for evaluation of a lump in his right testis. About 1
month ago, while taking a shower, he noted a hard area in his right testis that felt "like a
marble." He had never noticed this before and decided to wait and see if anything would
change. When the mass did not go away, he scheduled this appointment. Today, he states the
lump is not painful or tender to the touch and has not changed in size. He has had annual
physical exams and was never told that a lump was present. Four years ago, he had a scrotal
ultrasound following a brief episode of scrotal discomfort after competing in a bicycle race; the
result of the ultrasound was normal.

Review of Systems:
General: Overall feels well. Denies any weight loss, fevers, or chills.

Skin: Denies rashes, itching, or other lesions.

HEENT: Noncontributory

Pulmonary: No cough or shortness of breath.

Cardiovascular: No palpitations or chest pain.

Gastrointestinal: Good appetite, bowel movements are normal. Denies nausea or vomiting.
Denies abdominal or flank pain.

Genitourinary: No dysuria, hematuria, frequency, or urgency. No urethral discharge.

Musculoskeletal: No back or joint pain, no leg swelling.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: No reported medical history. Denies history of urinary tract infections, difficulty
with urination, immunosuppressive disorders, or sexually transmitted infections.

Surgical history: Rotator cuff repair 4 yr ago; left inguinal hernia repair as a child.

Medications: Occasional NSAIDs.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Mother and father healthy. No history of genitourinary malignancies in any
known relatives.

Social history: He denies current or previous tobacco use. He exercises almost every day with a
combination of weight training and cardio. He works primarily at a desk job with somewhat
frequent travel. All relevant immunizations are up to date. He denies exposure to any sick
contacts. He has had unprotected sex only with his wife for the past 3 yr.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Thin male who appears fatigued and older than stated age; in no apparent
respiratory distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 60 beats/min
BP: 112/65 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min
Height: 6'
Weight: 180 lb
BMI: 24.4

Skin: Warm and dry to the touch.

HEENT: Nasopharynx appears normal; no neck masses or lymphadenopathy.

Pulmonary: Breath sounds present and equal bilaterally. No stridor, rales, or wheezing.

Cardiovascular: Heart rate is regular; radial and dorsalis pedis pulses are present and equal
bilaterally; no pedal edema.

Gastrointestinal: Abdomen is not distended; there are no ecchymoses. Normal bowel sounds
are present. Abdomen is soft and nontender to light and deep palpation; no masses are present.

Genitourinary: Circumcised phallus, no visible lesions, bilateral descended testes. Left testis
smooth and nontender. Left epididymis is normal in texture and nontender. Right testis has firm
mass in the midsection that is nontender on palpation. Right epididymis is normal in texture and
nontender. There are no palpable inguinal lymph nodes. No urethral discharge.

Musculoskeletal: No costovertebral angle tenderness.

Neurologic: Unremarkable

Mental status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time.

Test Results:
result of the imaging study is shown. Which of the following
is a correct interpretation of the scrotal ultrasonography?

Cystic testicular mass

Hydrocele

Inguinal hernia

Normal

Solid testicular mass

criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.

criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 7-year-old girl presents with abrupt onset of fever, nausea, vomiting, and sore throat. The child denies cough, rhinorrhea, or nasal congestion. On physical exam, oral temperature is 101°F (38.5°C) and there is an exudative pharyngitis, with enlarged cervical lymph nodes. A rapid antigen test is positive for group A Streptococcus (GAS).

Age: 7
Sex: Female
Complaint: Abrupt onset of fever, nausea, vomiting, and sore throat with exudative pharyngitis and enlarged cervical lymph nodes.
Analysis: The clinical presentation of fever, exudative pharyngitis, and tender cervical lymphadenopathy in the absence of cough, rhinorrhea, or nasal congestion is highly characteristic of group A streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis. The positive rapid antigen detection test confirms the diagnosis. Main differential considerations include viral pharyngitis (less likely given the absence of coryza and cough and the presence of exudate and adenopathy) and other bacterial causes of exudative pharyngitis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (rapid antigen test already positive; throat culture not required for confirmation).
Conclusion: Confirmed group A streptococcal pharyngitis in a pediatric patient with classic clinical features and a positive rapid antigen test.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Initiate appropriate antibiotic therapy (e.g., penicillin or amoxicillin) for a full 10-day course to eradicate GAS, prevent acute rheumatic fever, and reduce transmission. Provide supportive care including antipyretics (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen) for fever and adequate hydration. Advise the child to remain home from school until 24 hours after starting antibiotics and clinical improvement. Educate the family on completing the full antibiotic course and on signs of complications (e.g., peritonsillar abscess, worsening symptoms). Schedule follow-up if symptoms do not improve within 48–72 hours.
Notes: None

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
case_text:
Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman with a history of Graves disease (non-compliant with methimazole for 2 months) presents with 2 days of palpitations, agitation, profuse sweating, and diarrhea. She had a dental extraction 3 days ago. On examination, she is markedly agitated, tremulous, and unable to remain still. Vital signs: T 40.0C (104F), HR 162 (atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response), RR 28, BP 168/60 (widened pulse pressure), SpO2 97%. She has a fine tremor, bilateral proptosis, lid lag, diffuse goiter with an audible bruit, and brisk reflexes throughout. Skin is warm and moist. She becomes increasingly confused during the examination. Labs: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 7.8 ng/dL (normal 0.8-1.8), free T3 22 pg/mL (normal 2.3-4.2). Burch-Wartofsky score is 65 (highly suggestive of thyroid storm). Propranolol, PTU, hydrocortisone, and iodine solution are initiated.
sc_draft_1:
Age: 32
Sex: Female
Complaint: Two days of palpitations, agitation, profuse sweating, and diarrhea in a patient with known Graves disease, with progressive confusion during examination.
Analysis: The patient has a history of Graves disease and has been non-compliant with methimazole for 2 months, with a recent dental extraction 3 days ago as a potential precipitant. She presents with classic hyperthyroid features: high fever (40.0C), tachycardia with atrial fibrillation and rapid ventricular response (HR 162), widened pulse pressure (BP 168/60), agitation, tremor, proptosis, lid lag, diffuse goiter with bruit, warm moist skin, and brisk reflexes. Labs confirm severe hyperthyroidism (TSH <0.01, free T4 7.8 ng/dL, free T3 22 pg/mL), and the Burch-Wartofsky score of 65 is highly suggestive of thyroid storm. The progressive confusion indicates central nervous system involvement, consistent with thyroid storm. Differential considerations include severe thyrotoxicosis versus thyroid storm, sepsis (given the recent dental extraction and fever), and pheochromocytoma (hypertension, sweating, tachycardia), though the clinical picture and Burch-Wartofsky score strongly favor thyroid storm.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring and telemetry; ECG to document and manage atrial fibrillation; serum electrolytes, glucose, calcium, and liver function tests (baseline before PTU); complete blood count; blood cultures (given fever and recent dental extraction); thyroid function tests already obtained; consider chest X-ray if respiratory status changes.
Conclusion: Thyroid storm (Burch-Wartofsky score 65) in a young woman with Graves disease, precipitated by medication non-compliance and recent dental extraction, complicated by atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and altered mental status.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: Admit to intensive care unit for continuous monitoring. Continue the initiated therapy: propranolol (high-dose beta-blockade for rate control and adrenergic symptoms), PTU (thionamide to block new hormone synthesis), hydrocortisone (to reduce T4-to-T3 conversion and treat relative adrenal insufficiency), and iodine solution (must be given at least 1 hour after PTU to avoid substrate for new hormone synthesis). Add aggressive cooling with acetaminophen and cooling blankets; avoid aspirin (displaces thyroid hormone from binding proteins). Provide intravenous fluids and electrolyte repletion. Evaluate and treat the precipitating factor, particularly possible infection from the dental extraction (obtain blood cultures and consider antibiotics if infection is confirmed). Monitor for arrhythmia, heart failure, and neurologic deterioration; consider rate control or cardioversion for atrial fibrillation as indicated. Continue antithyroid therapy and arrange endocrine follow-up for long-term management of Graves disease.
Notes: Iodine must be administered only after thionamide therapy to prevent worsening of thyrotoxicosis. Aspirin should be avoided. This is a life-threatening endocrine emergency requiring intensive care.

Vignette:
A 70-year-old man with a history of chronic HTN and atrial fibrillation is witnessed by a family member to have nausea, vomiting, and right-sided weakness, as well as difficulty speaking and comprehending language. sc_draft_1:
Age: 70  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Acute onset of nausea, vomiting, right-sided weakness, and difficulty speaking and comprehending language, progressing over minutes to severe aphasia and right arm paralysis.  
Analysis: The patient presents with acute focal neurological deficits (right hemiparesis and aphasia) consistent with a left hemispheric stroke. His history of atrial fibrillation and chronic hypertension, along with warfarin use, strongly suggests a cardioembolic etiology. The rapid progression over minutes is typical of an evolving ischemic stroke, but hemorrhagic transformation or primary intracerebral hemorrhage must be excluded, especially given anticoagulation. Differential diagnoses include acute ischemic stroke (large vessel occlusion), intracerebral hemorrhage, and less likely transient ischemic attack or seizure with Todd’s paresis. Urgent neuroimaging is essential to differentiate ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke and to guide reperfusion therapy.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Non-contrast CT head (urgent), CT angiography (if large vessel occlusion suspected), INR, blood glucose, complete blood count, electrolytes, ECG, and continuous vital sign monitoring.  
Conclusion: Acute ischemic stroke (likely cardioembolic) involving the left middle cerebral artery territory, with a high risk of hemorrhagic conversion due to warfarin therapy. Immediate emergent evaluation and management are required.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Neurology  
Recommendations: Immediately transfer to an emergency department with stroke capability. Perform urgent non-contrast CT head to rule out hemorrhage. Check INR and blood glucose. If within the thrombolytic window (≤4.5 hours from symptom onset) and INR ≤1.7, consider intravenous thrombolysis; otherwise, if INR >1.7 or hemorrhage is present, thrombolysis is contraindicated. Evaluate for mechanical thrombectomy if CT angiography shows a large vessel occlusion. Reverse anticoagulation (e.g., vitamin K, prothrombin complex concentrate) if hemorrhage is identified. Maintain blood pressure within guideline targets, monitor for neurological deterioration, and admit to a stroke unit.  
Notes: The exact time of symptom onset is critical for reperfusion decisions; the family member witnessed the onset, so the last known well time is the start of symptoms. Warfarin use significantly complicates thrombolytic therapy, and INR must be obtained urgently.

Sex: Male

Complaint: Acute onset of nausea, vomiting, right-sided weakness, difficulty speaking and comprehending language, progressing over minutes from mild slurred speech to severe aphasia and right arm paralysis, in a man with chronic hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and warfarin use.

Analysis: The acute, progressive onset of focal neurological deficits (right-sided weakness, aphasia, comprehension difficulty) localizes to the left middle cerebral artery territory. The patient's atrial fibrillation is a major cardioembolic source, making acute ischemic stroke the leading consideration. However, the concurrent warfarin use raises the critical differential of hemorrhagic stroke (intracerebral hemorrhage) due to over-anticoagulation. The rapid progression over minutes is consistent with either large-vessel occlusion or expanding hemorrhage. Nausea and vomiting may accompany increased intracranial pressure, which can occur in both ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke. The key distinguishing factor is urgent neuroimaging, as thrombolytic or thrombectomy decisions depend on excluding hemorrhage. Other considerations include seizure with Todd's paresis or a transient ischemic attack, but the sustained, progressive deficits make stroke most likely.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Non-contrast CT head (stat) to differentiate ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke; INR and PT/PTT to assess warfarin effect; complete blood count; serum glucose; basic metabolic panel; ECG; CT angiography (if ischemic stroke confirmed and within thrombectomy window); NIH Stroke Scale assessment.

Conclusion: This is a high-probability acute stroke presentation (likely left MCA territory) in a patient with atrial fibrillation on warfarin. The immediate priority is emergent neuroimaging to distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic etiology, as management diverges sharply (thrombolysis/thrombectomy vs. reversal of anticoagulation). Time-critical intervention is required.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Neurology

Recommendations: Activate the acute stroke pathway immediately. Obtain a stat non-contrast CT head and point-of-care INR. Maintain airway, breathing, and circulation; place patient on continuous cardiac monitoring. Do not administer antithrombotic or thrombolytic therapy until hemorrhage is excluded by imaging. If CT confirms ischemic stroke, assess eligibility for IV thrombolysis (alteplase/tenecteplase) or mechanical thrombectomy within the appropriate time windows, considering the elevated INR from warfarin as a contraindication to thrombolysis if INR >1.7. If CT shows hemorrhage, reverse anticoagulation emergently (e.g., vitamin K, prothrombin complex concentrate) and consult neurosurgery. Check blood glucose to rule out hypoglycemia as a mimic. Admit to a stroke unit or intensive care unit for monitoring of neurological status, blood pressure management per stroke guidelines, and dysphagia screening.

Notes: The patient's warfarin use is a critical caveat—thrombolysis is contraindicated with INR >1.7, and hemorrhagic transformation risk is elevated. Time from symptom onset (last known well) must be established precisely, as it determines treatment eligibility. Do not lower blood pressure acutely unless hemorrhage is confirmed or thrombolysis is planned.

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
case_text:
Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman presents with a cluster of small blisters on her lower lip that appeared today. She reports a tingling and burning sensation in the area that started yesterday. She has experienced similar episodes approximately twice a year for the past 5 years. She notes she has been under increased stress at work. She denies fever, sore throat, or oral ulcers. On examination, there is a cluster of small fluid-filled vesicles on an erythematous base on the left lower lip at the vermilion border. There is no facial nerve involvement, no lymphadenopathy, and no intraoral lesions.

Sex: Female

Analysis: The presentation of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base at the vermilion border, preceded by prodromal tingling/burning, recurrent episodes twice a year, and stress trigger, is classic for herpes simplex labialis (HSV-1). No systemic symptoms, intraoral lesions, lymphadenopathy, or facial nerve involvement, making complications unlikely. Differential includes impetigo, contact dermatitis, and aphthous ulcer (though the latter is intraoral), but the vesicular cluster on the lip with prodrome strongly supports herpes labialis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Recurrent herpes simplex labialis (cold sore) in an otherwise healthy young woman.

Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Consider topical antiviral (e.g., acyclovir cream) or oral antiviral (e.g., valacyclovir) if initiated early. Symptomatic relief with cold compresses and petroleum jelly. Advise to avoid touching/scratching, wash hands frequently, and avoid kissing or sharing utensils. Stress management. If episodes are frequent or severe, discuss suppressive therapy. Reassure that the condition is self-limiting.
Notes: If lesions become widespread, persist >2 weeks, or occur in immunocompromised patients, further evaluation is needed. Consider HSV-2 if genital involvement is present, but not in this case.

criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol

If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 50-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of worsening lower back pain radiating bilaterally to both legs, progressive bilateral leg weakness, and difficulty urinating since yesterday. He has a history of lumbar disc disease with two prior episodes of sciatica managed conservatively. On examination, he walks with a wide-based unsteady gait. Vital signs are within normal limits. Neurological exam reveals decreased strength (3/5) in bilateral ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, diminished patellar and absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally, and decreased perianal sensation with reduced anal sphincter tone on rectal exam. Post-void residual bladder scan shows 650 mL of retained urine. MRI of the lumbar spine reveals a large L4-L5 central disc herniation with severe compression of the cauda equina nerve roots.
